title: Safe CPU/GPU Temp for Overclocking + Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Safe Overclocking Temperature: How Much Thermal Margin Do You Have?
description: Is your CPU or GPU too hot to overclock? Enter your temperature under load and see how much thermal margin you have before throttling. Tjmax table by component.
seoKeywords: how hot is too hot for cpu
answerSnippet: For stable overclocking you need at least 10-15°C of margin below your component's maximum temperature (Tjmax). Typical Tjmax: Intel Core ~100°C, AMD Ryzen ~95°C, NVIDIA GPU ~90-93°C, AMD Radeon GPU ~110°C. Thermal margin = Tjmax − your temperature under load. Example: a Ryzen at 78°C (Tjmax 95°C) has 17°C of margin, enough for moderate overclocking.
intro: Every CPU and GPU has a **maximum temperature (Tjunction/Tjmax)** where **thermal throttling** kicks in (it lowers frequency to protect itself). For stable overclocking, you want to stay at least **10-15°C below** that limit under sustained load. This calculator takes your current temperature under load and the ambient temperature, and tells you exactly how much **thermal margin** you have for safe overclocking.
keyTakeaway: **Intel Core: Tjmax ~100°C · AMD Ryzen: ~95°C · NVIDIA GPU: ~90-93°C · AMD Radeon GPU: ~110°C.** Thermal margin = Tjmax − your temperature under load. You want ≥15°C of margin for stable OC.
useCases: You want to overclock and need to know if your cooler can handle it.
Your CPU hits 90°C under load and you want to know if it's dangerous.
You're choosing between an air cooler and a liquid AIO.
You want to know if thermal throttling is causing your low performance or FPS drops.
You're wondering if replacing thermal paste is worth it.

faq.q: What temperature does my CPU throttle at?
faq.a: **Intel Core**: ~100°C (Tjunction). **AMD Ryzen 7000/9000**: 95°C. When they reach this temperature they automatically lower frequency to protect themselves. On GPUs, throttling starts around 90-93°C on NVIDIA and up to 110°C on AMD Radeon.

For normal use, 80°C under heavy load is **acceptable**. For stable overclocking you ideally want to stay below 85°C: a Ryzen (Tjmax 95°C) at 80°C has 15°C of margin, right at the moderate-OC limit. An Intel chip (Tjmax 100°C) at 80°C has 20°C, which is more comfortable.

faq.q: How much thermal margin do I need for overclocking?
faq.a: At least **10-15°C below Tjmax** under sustained load. Margin >20°C: you can raise voltage/frequency. 15-20°C: stable moderate OC. 10-15°C: safe for normal use but not for OC. Under 10°C: risk of throttling, improve cooling before changing anything.

faq.q: Should I use air cooling or a liquid AIO for overclocking?
faq.a: For a non-overclocked CPU, a good air cooler (Noctua NH-D15, be quiet! Dark Rock) is enough. For moderate OC, a **240-280mm** AIO. For aggressive OC on an i9/Ryzen 9, a **360mm** runs 5-10°C cooler than air.

faq.q: How often should I replace thermal paste?
faq.a: Every **2-3 years**, or when you notice temperatures 5°C+ higher than before at the same load. Premium paste (Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut, Noctua NT-H1) lasts longer and runs 2-4°C cooler than generic paste.

faq.q: Does ambient temperature affect CPU temperature?
faq.a: Yes: roughly **1°C higher ambient = 1°C higher CPU/GPU**. On a hot summer day without AC (35°C), your PC can run up to 10°C hotter than in winter, so leave margin for the worst case.

faq.q: What is delta T in PC cooling?
faq.a: Delta T is the difference between your component temperature and the ambient temperature. A delta T of 53°C with 25°C ambient = 78°C component. It lets you compare coolers fairly: the same cooler gives the same delta T regardless of climate.

faq.q: Can overclocking permanently damage your CPU?
faq.a: Sustained high temperatures and excessive voltage **reduce lifespan** and can degrade the chip. With safe temperatures (≥15°C margin) and moderate voltage (Intel <1.45V, Ryzen 7000 <1.35V), overclocking is safe.

faq.q: How do I measure temperature under load correctly?
faq.a: Use **HWiNFO64, Core Temp or GPU-Z**, running sustained load for 10+ minutes: Cinebench R23 or AIDA64 for CPU, FurMark or a demanding game for GPU. Don't look at 30-second peaks — what matters is the steady-state temperature.

faq.q: What is the best CPU temperature while gaming?
faq.a: While gaming, **70-80°C** is ideal for most CPUs and GPUs. If you consistently hit 90°C+, improve case airflow, clean the dust, or undervolt to drop 5-10°C without losing performance.

howToSteps.name: Measure temperature under load
howToSteps.text: Use HWiNFO64, Core Temp or GPU-Z to read the max temp under sustained stress (Cinebench R23, AIDA64, FurMark, 10+ minutes).

howToSteps.text: Measure or estimate your room temperature (a thermometer or the day's weather works).

howToSteps.text: Check the thermal margin and status to know if you can overclock safely.

explanation:
## Safe Overclocking Temperature

Every CPU/GPU has a **maximum rated temperature (Tjunction/Tjmax)** at which **thermal throttling** activates: the chip reduces its clock frequency automatically to protect itself from permanent damage. For stable overclocking you need to maintain a **thermal margin of at least 15°C below that limit under sustained load**.

---

## How the margin is calculated

The formula is direct:

> **Thermal Margin = Tjmax − Temperature under sustained load**

**Real example:** An Intel Core i9-13900K has a Tjmax of 100°C. If under Cinebench R23 multicore (20 minutes) your CPU reaches 88°C:

> Thermal Margin = 100°C − 88°C = **12°C** → "tight" zone, not recommended for OC without improving cooling first.

The same math applies to GPUs: an RTX 4080 with a Tjmax of 93°C running at 74°C under FurMark has **19°C of margin** → green zone for moderate OC.

---

## Tjmax and sweet spot by component

> **Note on AMD Radeon:** AMD reports two different temperatures — *Edge* (PCB surface, ~20°C lower) and *Junction* (the die's real hotspot). Always use **Junction** to assess your true margin. Tools like HWiNFO64 clearly tell them apart.

---

## How to read your thermal margin

| Thermal margin | Meaning | Recommended action |
|---|---|---|
| **> 25°C** | Excellent, cooling headroom to spare | Moderate to aggressive OC viable |
| **15–25°C** | Good | Stable moderate OC |
| **5–15°C** | Tight | Very limited OC; improve cooling first |
| **< 5°C** | Critical | Do NOT overclock — risk of constant throttling |

---

## Relevant technical context

**Why 15°C and not 10°C?** Ambient temperature varies. In summer, a room can go from 20°C to 30°C. Since CPU temperature tracks ambient temperature roughly 1:1 (assuming the same TDP and airflow), that 10°C seasonal swing lands directly on the die. A 15°C margin gives you real coverage for those variations without the system throttling.

**Tjmax is not the permanent-damage limit.** It is the activation point for throttling as a protection mechanism. Electromigration damage in modern silicon occurs at considerably higher temperatures and/or with sustained elevated voltages. Constant throttling, however, wipes out any overclocking gains, which makes Tjmax the practical operating limit.

**Voltage amplifies the thermal problem.** Raising Vcore from 1.25V to 1.35V can increase effective TDP by 20–30% on modern architectures, since power scales with V². That means the same cooler that used to leave a 20°C margin could be down to just 8°C after an aggressive voltage bump.

---

## Recommended measurement tools (free)

- **HWiNFO64** – the reference for CPU and GPU monitoring on Windows; distinguishes Tdie, Tctl and individual per-core sensors.
- **Cinebench R23 / R24** – sustained CPU load; use the 10-minute minimum mode for steady state.
- **AIDA64 Extreme** – configurable stress test; useful for stressing CPU + memory + VRM simultaneously.
- **FurMark / 3DMark Stress Test** – sustained GPU load.
- **Throttlestop / Intel XTU** – to monitor whether throttling is active ("PL1", "Thermal" logs in Throttlestop).

---

## What this calculator does NOT include

- **Voltage (Vcore/Vgpu):** the thermal margin tells you whether you have headroom, but voltage determines how much heat you'll generate when raising frequencies. They must be evaluated together.
- **Memory stability (XMP/EXPO):** RAM module and IMC temperatures are separate variables.
- **Long-term degradation:** consistently operating above 90°C on Intel 13th/14th gen CPUs was one of the factors associated with the degradation issue documented in 2024 (related to eTVB voltages and uncapped power limits). High temperature + high voltage = higher risk of accelerated degradation.

---

## Common mistakes

- **Measuring with short benchmarks:** steady-state temperatures take 8–15 minutes to stabilize. A 30-second peak can read 10–15°C cooler than the real steady state.
- **Ignoring the motherboard VRM:** on mid-range boards, the VRM can reach 90–110°C before the CPU itself does, causing power throttling even when the die temperature isn't critical.
- **Confusing Tctl with Tdie on Ryzen:** some models report Tctl with a +10°C offset over the real temperature. HWiNFO64 applies the correction automatically; other tools don't.
- **Not recalculating the margin after changing thermal paste or the cooler:** thermal resistance (°C/W) changes with every intervention; always re-validate under sustained load.

example.title: Real example: Ryzen 7 7700X under load
steps: **Data**: Component = AMD Ryzen CPU, Tjmax = 95°C, current temperature under load = 78°C, ambient = 25°C.
**Delta T**: 78 − 25 = 53°C above ambient (a correct mid-range cooler).
**Recommendation**: You can raise PBO +100 MHz or PPT/TDC +5%. Verify each change with sustained Cinebench.
example.result: 17°C margin: safe for moderate overclocking with reasonable thermal error margin.
